lessons.title: Make adjectives match gender
lessons.explanation: Many Spanish adjectives change their ending to match a noun's grammatical gender. A common pattern is -o with masculine nouns and -a with feminine nouns. The noun decides the form.
lessons.trap_note: The ending follows the noun, not the person speaking: una persona cansada can describe anyone.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on standard Spanish noun-adjective agreement described in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española (concordancia).

lessons.title: Make words match singular or plural
lessons.explanation: When a noun is plural, its article and describing adjective usually become plural too. Add -s after a vowel, or often -es after a consonant.
lessons.trap_note: Check the whole noun phrase: los libros interesante still needs a plural adjective, interesantes.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on standard Spanish number agreement and plural formation described in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española.

lessons.title: Use ser for identity and origin
lessons.explanation: Use ser to say who or what someone is, where someone is from, and many lasting descriptions. Match the form of ser to the subject.
lessons.trap_note: A job or identity normally uses ser: Soy profesor. A current feeling usually uses estar.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on the standard distinction between ser and estar in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española and Diccionario panhispánico de dudas.

lessons.title: Use estar for states and location
lessons.explanation: Use estar for a current state or condition and for the location of people and things. The form of estar changes with the subject.
lessons.trap_note: An event's location usually uses ser: La clase es en el aula. A person's location uses estar.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on the standard distinction between ser and estar in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española and Diccionario panhispánico de dudas.

lessons.title: Build sentences with gustar
lessons.explanation: With gustar, the thing liked is the subject. Use gusta with one thing or an infinitive, and gustan with plural things. Add me, te, le, nos, or les for the person who likes it.

examples.es: A Luis le gustan los gatos.

lessons.trap_note: The verb agrees with the thing liked: me gustan las películas, because películas is plural.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on Spanish indirect-object constructions with gustar and verb agreement described in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española.

lessons.title: Match the present-tense verb ending
lessons.explanation: Regular present-tense verbs use different endings for each subject. For -ar verbs, yo often ends in -o; nosotros ends in -amos. -er and -ir verbs use their own patterns.
lessons.trap_note: Do not leave a conjugated verb in the infinitive after a subject: yo hablar needs to be yo hablo.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on regular present indicative conjugation patterns in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española.

lessons.title: Use a past tense for a finished event
lessons.explanation: For a completed event at a finished time, Spanish often uses the preterite. Use the present for habits and things happening now. Time words can help you choose.

examples.en: On Saturday we ate with Ana.

lessons.trap_note: A finished time such as ayer points toward a past form; a routine such as todos los días points toward the present.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on standard uses of the preterite and present indicative described in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española.

lessons.title: Choose an article that matches the noun
lessons.explanation: Spanish articles show whether a noun is specific or introduced for the first time. El and la mean 'the'; un and una often mean 'a'. Their form matches the noun's gender and number.
lessons.trap_note: A singular countable noun often needs an article: Tengo bicicleta is usually Tengo una bicicleta.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on standard Spanish article forms and noun phrase agreement described in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española.

lessons.title: Choose por or para from the meaning
lessons.explanation: Para often points to a goal, destination, recipient, or deadline. Por often gives a reason, route, duration, or exchange. Look at the relationship the sentence expresses.

examples.en: I study in order to learn.

lessons.trap_note: Translate the idea, not just the English word 'for': a goal uses para, while a cause often uses por.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on the standard meanings and contrasts of por and para described in the RAE Diccionario panhispánico de dudas.

lessons.title: Use an accent when it changes the word
lessons.explanation: Written accents show stress in some words and distinguish some short words with different meanings. They are part of the spelling, even when the word is short.

examples.en: What do you want? Tell me yes.

lessons.trap_note: Question words such as qué carry an accent in direct or indirect questions; the conjunction que does not.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on Spanish accentuation and diacritical accents described in the RAE Ortografía de la lengua española.

lessons.title: Keep a clear basic word order
lessons.explanation: A common Spanish sentence order is subject, verb, then object. Spanish can leave out a subject pronoun when the verb ending already makes the subject clear. Many adjectives follow the noun.
lessons.trap_note: A subject pronoun is not needed in every sentence: hablo already tells us the speaker is 'I'.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on common Spanish clause order, subject omission and adjective placement described in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española.

lessons.title: Use a before a person and a destination
lessons.explanation: Spanish uses a for many destinations and before a specific person who is the direct object. Use en for the place where someone or something is located.
lessons.trap_note: The personal a is for a person, not an ordinary object: veo el libro, but veo a mi profesor.
lessons.source_note: Original wording based on the personal a and place expressions described in the RAE Nueva gramática de la lengua española and Diccionario panhispánico de dudas.
